aspectTitle: Accessible name does not contain the visible label text (F111 / label-in-name overlap, 4.1.2 limb)
aspectDescription: A control has BOTH a visible text label AND a non-empty accessible name, but the accessible name omits, contradicts, or wholly replaces the words a sighted user reads on the control. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule (97a4e1 Button, e086e5 Form field, c487ae Link, 59796f Image button, m6b1q3 Menuitem, 2t702h Summary) terminates the instant accName !== ""; none compare the computed name STRING against the rendered visible label STRING. F111 maps explicitly to 4.1.2 (its title is 'Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name') and de
scenario: SaaS document-editor toolbar: the primary action button visibly reads 'Save' but carries aria-label='Persist document to server', so the visible word 'Save' appears nowhere in the accessible name. Verified in Chromium: role=button, accName='Persist document to server'.
mechanism: aria-label on a native <button> overrides and suppresses the child text node 'Save'; the accessible name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role is correct, but it omits the visible label, so a speech-input user saying 'click Save' matches nothing and a screen-reader user gets no anchor to the on-screen word. F111 check #3 (accName must contain the visible label) fails.

aspectTitle: Accessible name is present but uninformative / does not communicate the control's purpose (ARIA14 name-quality)
aspectDescription: A user-interface control has a non-empty, machine-valid accessible name, but the name does not identify what the control DOES — it is placeholder text, an asset filename, a developer string, or a generic token duplicated across distinct controls. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule is scoped to non-emptiness only and explicitly does not assess descriptiveness, so a name like 'button', 'icon_search_24px.svg', 'TODO label', or five identical 'star' labels passes uniformly. ARIA14 sets the actual bar: 'users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of compon
scenario: Document-editor formatting toolbar of five icon-only buttons (cut, copy, paste, undo, redo), each rendering a distinct SVG glyph and performing a distinct action, but all carrying the identical accessible name aria-label="button". A screen-reader user hears "button, button, button, button, button" and cannot distinguish function.
mechanism: AccName of all five buttons computes to "button" (from aria-label, overriding the aria-hidden SVG). Non-empty and role-correct so the ACT 'Button has non-empty accessible name' rule passes, but the generic token conveys no purpose — verified via Chrome CDP accessibility tree: five buttons all named "button".

scenario: Real-estate CRM 'edit contact' panel with three contentEditable <div role="textbox"> fields — mailing address, internal notes, follow-up reminder — each with a visible <h3> heading above it, but all sharing the identical accessible name aria-label="editor". aspectTitle: Role is syntactically valid but is the wrong role for the control's appearance/behavior (F15/F59 semantic variant)
aspectDescription: An interactive element carries a role that is a real ARIA token (so 674b10 'Role attribute has valid value' passes) and whose required states are present (so 4e8ab6 passes), but the role is WRONG for what the element actually is and does. A sliding toggle switch coded role="checkbox", a control that depresses and fires an in-page action coded role="link", an operable disclosure header marked role="heading", a clickable star coded role="img". F59's literal failure is a div/span with NO role (axe-core flags clickable-with-no-role); the genuinely uncovered, automation-resistant case is a VALID bu
scenario: Northwind Postmaster notification settings: sliding pill toggle switches (thumb-on-track, green=on/grey=off, instant effect) coded as div role=checkbox with aria-checked. Visually/behaviourally a switch, announced as a checkbox.
mechanism: The control's rendered/behavioural identity is an on/off SWITCH (correct role=switch, announced 'on/off'), but it is coded role=checkbox (a valid ARIA token with its required aria-checked state present and synced), so AT announces 'checkbox, checked' — a form selection affordance rather than a live setting toggle. The role is valid but inappropriate for the widget.

The control performs an in-page action and never navigates (no href, no URL change), so the correct role is button. Announcing an in-page action control as a 'link' misleads AT users about what activation will do.

scenario: Cirro Weather display settings: a joined segmented control for temperature unit (°C / °F) where exactly one is always selected and choosing one deselects the other, but each segment is coded div role=button with aria-pressed.

scenario: Bibliothek (de-DE) settings boundary/PASS counterexample: an icon-only '✕' close that looks like a graphic but is a native button, a sliding night-mode switch correctly coded role=switch, and an operable disclosure correctly coded role=button — every role matches its rendered/behavioural identity.

aspectTitle: Exposed ARIA state/value is present and valid but contradicts the rendered control state (value correctness, not presence)
aspectDescription: A custom control exposes a state/value (aria-checked, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-valuenow) that is a permitted, syntactically-valid value (so 4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281 all pass) but that does not match the control's CURRENT visible state: a toggle rendered ON with aria-checked="false", an accordion visibly expanded with aria-expanded="false", a highlighted active tab while aria-selected stays on the first tab, a slider thumb at max with aria-valuenow="0". SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'can be programmatically set' AND that 'notification of changes... is available'; a
scenario: A Meridian Bank Security Alerts & Notifications settings screen. The first custom role="switch" toggle ("Sign-in alerts") is rendered unmistakably ON (green track, thumb pushed right via the .is-on class) while its exposed state is hard-coded aria-checked="false"; the other two switches are genuinely off. Browser-confirmed: visual ON, aria-checked=false.
mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-checked. role=switch, accessible name, and a permitted/valid boolean are all present, so a screen reader announces the visibly-ON switch as 'Sign-in alerts, switch, off' — the exact inverse of the rendered state; a voice-control user toggles it expecting to turn it on and instead turns it off. SC 4.1.2's 'keep up to date on the status' requirement fails because AT receives the wrong value.

aspectTitle: Accessible name/text alternative on a dynamic named component goes stale after the content changes (F20, temporal correctness)
aspectDescription: A named or interactive component whose visual content is swapped by script (a status-icon button, a favorite/star toggle, a refreshable image control, a rotating banner acting as a named region) keeps its accessible name/alt frozen on the OLD content. F20 is explicit: 'the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time.' The name was once correct and is non-empty, so every presence rule passes when sampled once; after the state change it describes a different thing than what is rendered. aspectTitle: Each part of a multi-part field has a present but ambiguous/undifferentiated sub-name (F86 semantic variant)
aspectDescription: A compound field (US phone as 3 inputs, date as day/month/year, credit card in 4 groups, time as hour/minute/AM-PM) gives EACH sub-input a non-empty accessible name (so e086e5 passes on every part) — but the per-part names fail to convey each part's role within the whole: all three phone parts named 'Phone', a date's three fields all named 'Date', or area-code and prefix both named 'Number'. F86's intent is that without correctly differentiated per-part names users experience 'undefined text fields'; the automation-resistant case is when names exist but are interchangeable/unhelpful. scenario: E-commerce checkout (Trailhead Outfitters) mobile-number field built as three boxes laid out '( 402 ) 555 - 0173'. Visual parentheses/dash make the area/prefix/line structure obvious, but all three inputs carry the identical aria-label="Phone".

Chrome AX tree confirms three textboxes all named exactly 'Phone'.

scenario: SaaS billing page (Lumen Studio) 'Add a payment method' enters a 16-digit card number as four ordered four-digit boxes rendered '4242 .. 4242 .. 4242 .. 4242', component-library style in a <div role=group>; every box carries aria-label="Card number".
mechanism: Each of the four segment inputs has the non-empty name 'Card number' (e086e5 passes per-field), but the four identical names lose the 'which segment' information a sighted user gets from position and the gaps; the only segment cues are visual order plus aria-hidden .sep spacers. Auto-advance compounds it. Chrome AX tree confirms four textboxes all named 'Card number'.

aspectTitle: Each part of a multi-part field has a present but ambiguous/undifferentiated sub-name (F86 semantic variant)
aspectDescription: A compound field (US phone as 3 inputs, date as day/month/year, credit card in 4 groups, time as hour/minute/AM-PM) gives EACH sub-input a non-empty accessible name (so e086e5 passes on every part) — but the per-part names fail to convey each part's role within the whole: all three phone parts named 'Phone', a date's three fields all named 'Date', or area-code and prefix both named 'Number'. F86's intent is that without correctly differentiated per-part names users experience 'undefined text fields'; the automation-resistant case is when names exist but are interchangeable/unhelpful. Deciding
scenario: Japanese municipal portal registration: postal code (郵便番号) entered as a 3-digit and a 4-digit box joined by a hyphen and written 〒 123-4567; both boxes carry the identical aria-label="郵便番号" (postal code).
mechanism: Each of the two postal-code blocks has the non-empty name '郵便番号' (e086e5 passes per-field), but the two identical names cannot identify the first-three-digits block (上3桁) vs the last-four block (下4桁); the 〒 mark, hyphen, and 上3桁/下4桁 captions are all aria-hidden. Chrome AX tree confirms two textboxes both named '郵便番号'.

Deciding
scenario: Cardiology patient portal (Northgate Cardiology) logs a home blood-pressure reading written '128 / 82 mmHg' as a systolic input, a diastolic input, and a unit <select>; all three controls derive their accessible name from title="Blood pressure" (no label/aria-label).
mechanism: The title attribute supplies a non-empty accessible name 'Blood pressure' to both number inputs and the unit combobox (e086e5 passes per-field), but the three identical names cannot identify systolic (top/higher) vs diastolic (bottom/lower) vs the unit — a clinically critical distinction. The 'Systolic'/'Diastolic' captions and '/' separator are aria-hidden. Chrome AX tree confirms two textboxes and one combobox all named 'Blood pressure'.

Deciding
scenario: B2B account 'Contact preferences' page (Meridian Logistics) collects an international work phone as three boxes '+ 44 20 - 7946 0991', built correctly per the ARIA14 multi-field example: each part has a distinct role-appropriate aria-label (country code / area code / subscriber number) inside a role=group captioned 'Work phone'. PASS boundary contrast.
mechanism: Same multi-part structural shape as the failing cases, but each sub-input has a DISTINCT, role-appropriate accessible name plus matching autocomplete tel token, so a user landing on any single box knows exactly which segment it is. Chrome AX tree confirms three textboxes named 'country code', 'area code', 'subscriber number' respectively. This isolates the aspect: the failure under test is undifferentiated naming, not the presence of a multi-part field.
